title: Resiliency, Security & Architecture Patterns
summary: Resiliency patterns (circuit breaker 3-state machine, retry with jitter, bulkhead), security internals (TLS 1.3, JWT, OAuth 2.0), and cloud architecture patterns.

explanation.overview: Real production systems fail constantly. Resilient systems don't prevent all failures — they isolate them, recover quickly, and degrade gracefully. Security ensures that only authorized users can access data and that data is protected in transit and at rest. Architecture patterns provide reusable solutions for common system evolution challenges.

key_concepts.definition: INTERNAL: CLOSED (normal): requests pass through. Track failure count. When failures reach threshold (e.g., 5 failures in 60 seconds), transition to OPEN. OPEN: all requests fail immediately (fast-fail) without calling the downstream service. After a timeout period (e.g., 30 seconds), transition to HALF-OPEN. HALF-OPEN: allow ONE probe request through. If it succeeds, transition back to CLOSED (service recovered). If it fails, transition back to OPEN (still down). INTERNAL STATE: {state: CLOSED|OPEN|HALF_OPEN, failure_count: int, last_failure_time: timestamp, success_count_in_half_open: int}. CONFIGURABLE: failure_threshold (5), timeout_duration (30s), success_threshold_in_half_open (3). WHY: prevents cascading failures. If Service B is down, Service A's circuit breaker fast-fails instead of timing out on every request (saving thread pool resources and response time). TOOLS: Resilience4j (Java), Polly (.NET), Hystrix (deprecated Netflix), Envoy (built-in circuit breaking).

On transient failure (network timeout, 503), retry after increasing delays. Formula: wait = min(cap, base × 2^attempt) + random_jitter. Example: base=100ms, cap=30s. Attempt 1: 100ms + jitter. Attempt 2: 200ms + jitter. Attempt 3: 400ms + jitter. ... Attempt 8: 25.6s + jitter. WHY JITTER: without jitter, all clients that failed at the same time retry at the same time (thundering herd retry storm). Jitter spreads retries randomly. Types: Full jitter: wait = random(0, min(cap, base × 2^attempt)). Equal jitter: wait = min(cap, base × 2^attempt)/2 + random(0, min(cap, base × 2^attempt)/2). ONLY retry on transient errors (timeout, 503, 429). NEVER retry on permanent errors (400, 404, 403).

Isolate resources so failure in one area doesn't affect others. Named after ship bulkhead compartments. IMPLEMENTATION: separate thread pools per downstream service. Service A gets thread pool of 20. Service B gets thread pool of 20. If Service A is slow and all 20 threads are blocked, Service B's pool is unaffected — it continues serving normally. Without bulkhead: a slow downstream blocks all shared threads, and the entire server becomes unresponsive. Envoy proxy: configurable max_connections and max_pending_requests per upstream cluster.

ALWAYS set timeouts on every external call. Without timeouts, a hung downstream service blocks your threads indefinitely. DEADLINE PROPAGATION: pass the remaining time budget downstream. If the client set a 5-second deadline and your service spent 2 seconds so far, pass 3 seconds to the downstream call. If the downstream can't complete in 3 seconds, it fast-fails. gRPC has built-in deadline propagation. For REST: pass deadline as a header (X-Request-Deadline: unix_timestamp).

examples.title: Netflix Chaos Engineering & Hystrix Fallbacks
examples.description: How Netflix built the Simian Army to intentionally break production systems, forcing developers to build resilient software.
examples.code:
The Problem:
When Netflix migrated to AWS, they realized that in a massive distributed environment, EC2 instances drop, networks partition, and downstream dependencies periodically fail. Assuming 99.9% availability per microservice, a call chain of 100 microservices yields only 90.4% total uptime.

The Architecture (Hystrix & Chaos Monkey):
1. The Hystrix Circuit Breaker: Netflix built 'Hystrix' to wrap every external call in a circuit breaker with a strict timeout and an isolated thread pool (Bulkhead pattern). If a downstream recommendation service hung, Hystrix would instantly fast-fail the request rather than exhausting Netflix's Tomcat connection pool.
2. Graceful Fallbacks: When Hystrix tripped, it didn't just throw an error. It triggered a fallback function. If the 'personalized recommendations' service failed, Hystrix returned an old cached list, or a hardcoded list of 'Top 10 Globally' movies. The user never saw an error.
3. Chaos Monkey: To guarantee these fallbacks actually worked, Netflix created Chaos Monkey, a script that randomly terminated production EC2 instances during business hours. This forced engineers to design stateless, resilient microservices where the loss of any single node was invisible to the user.

Takeaway for Interviews:
True resiliency isn't about preventing servers from going down; it's about anticipating failure. Always design 'degraded modes.' If the search system fails, can you offer a basic category browse? If the database fails, can you serve a stale cache?

examples.title: Circuit Breaker Implementation in Python
examples.description: A bare-bones implementation of the 3-state Circuit Breaker state machine (Closed, Open, Half-Open).
examples.code:
import time
import random
from enum import Enum

class State(Enum):
    CLOSED = 1
    OPEN = 2
    HALF_OPEN = 3

class CircuitBreaker:
    def __init__(self, failure_threshold=3, recovery_timeout=5):
        self.state = State.CLOSED
        self.failure_threshold = failure_threshold
        self.recovery_timeout = recovery_timeout
        self.failures = 0
        self.last_failure_time = None

    def call(self, func, *args, **kwargs):
        if self.state == State.OPEN:
            if time.time() - self.last_failure_time > self.recovery_timeout:
                print("Timeout elapsed. State -> HALF_OPEN. Allowing 1 test request.")
                self.state = State.HALF_OPEN
            else:
                raise Exception("Circuit is OPEN. Fast-failing request.")

        try:
            result = func(*args, **kwargs)
            
            if self.state == State.HALF_OPEN:
                print("Half-Open test succeeded! State -> CLOSED. Resetting counters.")
                self.state = State.CLOSED
                self.failures = 0
            return result
            
        except Exception as e:
            self.failures += 1
            self.last_failure_time = time.time()
            print(f"Call failed. Failure {self.failures}/{self.failure_threshold}.")
            
            if self.failures >= self.failure_threshold:
                print("Threshold reached! State -> OPEN.")
                self.state = State.OPEN
            raise e

# Usage:
# cb = CircuitBreaker()
# try:
#     result = cb.call(fetch_data_from_flakey_payment_api, payload)
# except Exception:
#     result = get_cached_fallback_data()

examples.title: Resiliency Pattern Decision Matrix
examples.description: Which fault-tolerance pattern to apply in an interview based on the failure behavior of the downstream dependency.
examples.code:
FAILURE SCENARIO             | CORRECT PATTERN           | DESCRIPTION
-----------------------------|---------------------------|----------------------------------------------------
Transient Network Glitch     | Retry with Jitter/Backoff | Retry immediately, then wait longer. Add jitter to prevent storm.
Downstream DB is Dead        | Circuit Breaker           | Stop calling it. Fast-fail immediately. Periodically test (Half-Open).
Slow / Hung Downstream       | Timeouts + Bulkheads      | Strict deadlines. Isolate thread pools so a slow service doesn't drain caller.
Sudden Traffic Spike         | Rate Limiting / Load Shed | Drop requests shedding bottom-tier traffic to save core infrastructure.
Unavailable Crucial Service  | Graceful Fallback         | Serve stale cache, default data, or simplified UI instead of 500 Error.

configurable_params.default: Default library settings usually favor CP over AP
configurable_params.effect: You can modify connection timeouts, retry buffers, and max memory limits.
configurable_params.tradeoff: Tuning configuration to drop stale packets reduces latency but requires robust frontend exception handling.

key_concepts.definition: Stateless authentication token: Header.Payload.Signature (base64-encoded). Header: {alg: 'RS256', typ: 'JWT'}. Payload: {user_id: 123, role: 'admin', exp: 1710456789}. Signature: HMAC-SHA256(header + '.' + payload, secret_key) or RSA signature for asymmetric. VERIFICATION: server decodes header+payload, recomputes signature with its secret/public key, compares. If match, token is valid and untampered. STATELESS: no server-side session storage needed. Server doesn't need to query a database to verify identity. EDGE CASES: JWT can't be revoked before expiry (stateless = no server-side invalidation). FIX: use short expiry (15 min) + refresh tokens (stored server-side, revocable, long-lived). Or maintain a token blacklist in Redis (defeats stateless purpose but adds revocation). Token size: JWTs can grow large (1-4 KB) — stored in every request header. Don't put unnecessary data in the payload.

Standard for third-party authorization (Login with Google). Flow: (1) User clicks 'Login with Google' → redirect to Google's auth server with client_id + redirect_uri. (2) User authenticates on Google → Google redirects back to your app with an authorization_code. (3) Your BACKEND exchanges code + client_secret with Google's token endpoint → receives access_token + refresh_token. (4) Use access_token to call Google APIs on behalf of the user. PKCE extension (required for mobile/SPA): no client_secret. Instead, generate code_verifier (random string), send code_challenge = SHA256(code_verifier) in step 1. In step 3, send code_verifier — Google verifies it matches the challenge. Prevents authorization code interception attacks.

In Transit: TLS (HTTPS) encrypts all data between client and server. Use mTLS (mutual TLS) for service-to-service communication inside the cluster — both sides present certificates. At Rest: AES-256-GCM encryption for data stored on disk. Key management: use a KMS (AWS KMS, HashiCorp Vault) — application never handles raw encryption keys. Envelope encryption: KMS encrypts a data encryption key (DEK) → DEK encrypts the data → store encrypted DEK alongside encrypted data.

Traditional security: trust everything inside the network perimeter (VPN). Zero Trust: never trust, always verify. Every request must be authenticated and authorized, even between internal services. Implementation: mTLS between all services (Istio service mesh), per-request authorization (check JWT + RBAC on every API call), micro-segmentation (network policies limiting which services can talk to which), short-lived credentials (rotate certificates every 24 hours).

Incrementally migrate from a monolith to microservices. Place a facade (API Gateway) in front of the monolith. Gradually route endpoints from the monolith to new microservices. Old code is 'strangled' (replaced) one route at a time. At the end, the monolith is fully replaced. WHY: avoids the risk of a Big Bang rewrite. You can validate each microservice in production before moving the next endpoint. CONFIGURABLE: use feature flags or traffic splitting (route 10% of /orders to new service, 90% to monolith).

Deploy a helper process alongside the main application container (in the same pod in Kubernetes). The sidecar handles cross-cutting concerns: logging (Fluentd sidecar ships logs), monitoring (Prometheus sider), security (Envoy sidecar handles mTLS), traffic management (Istio sidecar proxies all network traffic). The main application is unaware of the sidecar — they communicate via localhost.

When integrating with a legacy system or third-party API that has a different domain model, add a translation layer. Your services communicate with the ACL, which translates between your clean domain model and the legacy model. Prevents legacy concepts from leaking into your codebase.

diagram.title: Circuit Breaker Pattern
diagram.description: Failing fast to prevent cascading system collapse.

data.mermaid_source:
stateDiagram-v2
  [*] --> Closed: Service Healthy
  Closed --> Open: Errors > Threshold (e.g. 50%)
  Open --> HalfOpen: Timeout Elapsed (30s)
  HalfOpen --> Closed: Success (Ping passes)
  HalfOpen --> Open: Failure (Still broken)
  
  note left of Closed
    Pass Requests Normally
  end note
  note right of Open
    Fail Fast! (Return 503 Instantly)
  end note
  note right of HalfOpen
    Let 1 request through to test
  end note
